raw_evidence.label: What 'top-100 most active' actually selects
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is the 100 games with the most recently verified runs as of 25 May 2026 — not the 100 most-popular games, not the 100 most-iconic, not the 100 with the most lifetime runs. This is a moving window. Three populations dominate the cut: (1) brand-new releases whose communities are still onboarding (Subnautica 2 hit Early Access on 14 May 2026, eleven days before the fetch, and tops the list); (2) recent blockbusters where the meta is still being figured out (Hollow Knight: Silksong, Hades 2, Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End); and (3) 'evergreen grinder' titles whose verification rate is dominated by a single dedicated community uploading hundreds of runs each (Granny: Legacy, multiple SpongeBob games, ROBLOX-engine titles, Geometry Dash). The 'casual canon' games — Super Mario 64, Hollow Knight, BotW, Undertale — appear too, but as second-rank presences rather than the top of the list.

raw_evidence.label: SpongeBob: an unlikely speedrun dynasty
raw_evidence.content: Eight separate SpongeBob entries appear in our top-100 ('Battle for Bikini Bottom' original and Rehydrated, plus Category Extensions for both, 'Cosmic Shake', 'Titans of the Tide', 'Big Guy Challenge', 'Basics! - Remastered', 'Destroy SpongeBob'). The series became a speedrun anchor after 'Battle for Bikini Bottom' was performed at AGDQ 2017 by the runner SHIFT, and PC Gamer profiled the community in 2020 as 'a surprisingly compelling bracket packed with enough nuance to seduce any aspiring speed player.' What this tells us about our top-100 cut: a single dedicated community can keep a 22-year-old kids' platformer above 'Super Mario 64' in terms of recent verification activity. The currently-most-active list rewards active grinders, not historical fame.

raw_evidence.label: Last 30 days: Granny: Legacy alone is 25%
raw_evidence.content: Of the 2,230 runs verified in the last 30 days before the fetch (26 April → 25 May 2026), Granny: Legacy is single-handedly responsible for 561 — over 25% of the entire top-100 verification activity. Hollow Knight: Silksong is next at 125 (5.6%), then Super Mario 64 (113), Hades 2 (90), Poppy Playtime: Chapter 1 (87), Block Tales (79). A single Slavic-dominated mobile horror leaderboard is contributing more verifications than the next four games combined.

Y1 = NOW - pd.Timedelta(days=365)
last30 = df[df["date_verified"] >= M1]
last365 = df[df["date_verified"] >= Y1]
g30 = last30.groupby("game_id").size().sort_values(ascending=False).head(15)
g365 = last365.groupby("game_id").size().sort_values(ascending=False).head(15)
print(f"\nTop 15 by runs in last 30 days (total: {len(last30)}):")
for gid, n in g30.items():
    print(f"  {n:>4}  {name_by_id.get(gid, gid)}")
print(f"\nTop 15 by runs in last 365 days (total: {len(last365)}):")
for gid, n in g365.items():
    print(f"  {n:>4}  {name_by_id.get(gid, gid)}")

raw_evidence.label: Origin of speedrun.com
raw_evidence.content: Speedrun.com was founded in March 2014 by Irish programmer Peter Chase, who goes by the username 'Pac'. It was designed with deliberately looser submission rules than the older Speed Demos Archive (SDA, 1998) and gave each game its own community-elected moderators rather than a single editorial board. The first migration was a wave of Grand Theft Auto runners; from there it grew into the de-facto central hub for speedrun leaderboards. In October 2020 Chase sold the site to Elo Entertainment, citing growth ambitions. By July 2021, Wikipedia reports the site hosted 'leaderboards for over 20,000 video games' — a five-year ramp from a single game's leaderboard to a multi-thousand-game commons.

raw_evidence.label: Verification: how a run becomes 'verified'
raw_evidence.content: Every run on a speedrun.com leaderboard exists in one of three states: pending, verified, or rejected. A submission must include video proof and is reviewed by the community-elected moderators of that specific game, who check splits, audio sync, glitch boundaries, and (for high-end runs) sometimes a handcam showing the player's hands on the controller. The site does not run a single global verification policy; each game's moderator team writes its own ruleset, defines its own categories, and decides what counts as proof. This is why the same dataset can contain a 4-minute Subnautica 2 glitched run and a 3-hour Silksong True Ending run, both stamped 'verified' — they are verified by completely different small teams of volunteers. The technical scaffolding that made this workable was YouTube (2005, video hosting) and Twitch (2011, livestream replays); together they let any moderator anywhere watch any submitted run frame by frame.

raw_evidence.label: What 'top-100 most active' actually selects
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is the 100 games with the most recently verified runs as of 25 May 2026 — not the 100 most-popular games, not the 100 most-iconic, not the 100 with the most lifetime runs. This is a moving window. Three populations dominate the cut: (1) brand-new releases whose communities are still onboarding (Subnautica 2 hit Early Access on 14 May 2026, eleven days before the fetch, and tops the list); (2) recent blockbusters where the meta is still being figured out (Hollow Knight: Silksong, Hades 2, Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End); and (3) 'evergreen grinder' titles whose verification rate is dominated by a single dedicated community uploading hundreds of runs each (Granny: Legacy, multiple SpongeBob games, ROBLOX-engine titles, Geometry Dash). The 'casual canon' games — Super Mario 64, Hollow Knight, BotW, Undertale — appear too, but as second-rank presences rather than the top of the list.

raw_evidence.label: Category fragmentation per game
raw_evidence.content: The 100 games in our cut spawn 608 per-game categories — a mean of 6.27 and a median of 5 per game. The maximum is 31 (Super Mario Bros. Category Extensions, an entire 'category-extensions' pseudo-game whose purpose is to track exotic side-categories), then 27 (Granny: Legacy), 20 (Papa Louie Category Extensions; MX Bikes), 16 (Undertale). 19 games carry 10 or more parallel leaderboards. At the other end, 7 games carry exactly one category (Bloons Tower Defense 6, Subnautica 2 in Early Access, Roblox: Alone, Chase, Final Ninja Zero, and others — usually newer or smaller communities). The implication: 'world record' is not one thing, it is roughly six things per game, each with its own #1 runner.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_07: category fragmentation — how many distinct categories per game ---
print("=== ana_07 ===")
pergame = categories[categories["type"] == "per-game"]
catcounts = pergame.groupby("game_id").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"per-game categories: {len(pergame)} across {pergame['game_id'].nunique()} games")
print(f"mean: {catcounts.mean():.2f}, median: {catcounts.median():.0f}, max: {catcounts.max()}, min: {catcounts.min()}")
print("\nTop 10 by category count:")
for gid, n in catcounts.head(10).items():
    print(f"  {n:>3}  {name_by_id.get(gid, gid)}")
print("\nBottom 5 (single category):")
for gid, n in catcounts.tail(5).items():
    print(f"  {n:>3}  {name_by_id.get(gid, gid)}")
print(f"\nGames with exactly 1 category: {(catcounts == 1).sum()}")
print(f"Games with >= 10 categories:   {(catcounts >= 10).sum()}")

raw_evidence.label: Origin of speedrun.com
raw_evidence.content: Speedrun.com was founded in March 2014 by Irish programmer Peter Chase, who goes by the username 'Pac'. It was designed with deliberately looser submission rules than the older Speed Demos Archive (SDA, 1998) and gave each game its own community-elected moderators rather than a single editorial board. The first migration was a wave of Grand Theft Auto runners; from there it grew into the de-facto central hub for speedrun leaderboards. In October 2020 Chase sold the site to Elo Entertainment, citing growth ambitions. By July 2021, Wikipedia reports the site hosted 'leaderboards for over 20,000 video games' — a five-year ramp from a single game's leaderboard to a multi-thousand-game commons.

raw_evidence.label: Origin of speedrun.com
raw_evidence.content: Speedrun.com was founded in March 2014 by Irish programmer Peter Chase, who goes by the username 'Pac'. It was designed with deliberately looser submission rules than the older Speed Demos Archive (SDA, 1998) and gave each game its own community-elected moderators rather than a single editorial board. The first migration was a wave of Grand Theft Auto runners; from there it grew into the de-facto central hub for speedrun leaderboards. In October 2020 Chase sold the site to Elo Entertainment, citing growth ambitions. By July 2021, Wikipedia reports the site hosted 'leaderboards for over 20,000 video games' — a five-year ramp from a single game's leaderboard to a multi-thousand-game commons.

raw_evidence.label: Verification: how a run becomes 'verified'
raw_evidence.content: Every run on a speedrun.com leaderboard exists in one of three states: pending, verified, or rejected. A submission must include video proof and is reviewed by the community-elected moderators of that specific game, who check splits, audio sync, glitch boundaries, and (for high-end runs) sometimes a handcam showing the player's hands on the controller. The site does not run a single global verification policy; each game's moderator team writes its own ruleset, defines its own categories, and decides what counts as proof. This is why the same dataset can contain a 4-minute Subnautica 2 glitched run and a 3-hour Silksong True Ending run, both stamped 'verified' — they are verified by completely different small teams of volunteers. The technical scaffolding that made this workable was YouTube (2005, video hosting) and Twitch (2011, livestream replays); together they let any moderator anywhere watch any submitted run frame by frame.

raw_evidence.label: What 'top-100 most active' actually selects
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is the 100 games with the most recently verified runs as of 25 May 2026 — not the 100 most-popular games, not the 100 most-iconic, not the 100 with the most lifetime runs. This is a moving window. Three populations dominate the cut: (1) brand-new releases whose communities are still onboarding (Subnautica 2 hit Early Access on 14 May 2026, eleven days before the fetch, and tops the list); (2) recent blockbusters where the meta is still being figured out (Hollow Knight: Silksong, Hades 2, Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End); and (3) 'evergreen grinder' titles whose verification rate is dominated by a single dedicated community uploading hundreds of runs each (Granny: Legacy, multiple SpongeBob games, ROBLOX-engine titles, Geometry Dash). The 'casual canon' games — Super Mario 64, Hollow Knight, BotW, Undertale — appear too, but as second-rank presences rather than the top of the list.

raw_evidence.label: Origin of speedrun.com
raw_evidence.content: Speedrun.com was founded in March 2014 by Irish programmer Peter Chase, who goes by the username 'Pac'. It was designed with deliberately looser submission rules than the older Speed Demos Archive (SDA, 1998) and gave each game its own community-elected moderators rather than a single editorial board. The first migration was a wave of Grand Theft Auto runners; from there it grew into the de-facto central hub for speedrun leaderboards. In October 2020 Chase sold the site to Elo Entertainment, citing growth ambitions. By July 2021, Wikipedia reports the site hosted 'leaderboards for over 20,000 video games' — a five-year ramp from a single game's leaderboard to a multi-thousand-game commons.

raw_evidence.label: Verification: how a run becomes 'verified'
raw_evidence.content: Every run on a speedrun.com leaderboard exists in one of three states: pending, verified, or rejected. A submission must include video proof and is reviewed by the community-elected moderators of that specific game, who check splits, audio sync, glitch boundaries, and (for high-end runs) sometimes a handcam showing the player's hands on the controller. The site does not run a single global verification policy; each game's moderator team writes its own ruleset, defines its own categories, and decides what counts as proof. This is why the same dataset can contain a 4-minute Subnautica 2 glitched run and a 3-hour Silksong True Ending run, both stamped 'verified' — they are verified by completely different small teams of volunteers. The technical scaffolding that made this workable was YouTube (2005, video hosting) and Twitch (2011, livestream replays); together they let any moderator anywhere watch any submitted run frame by frame.

raw_evidence.label: What 'top-100 most active' actually selects
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is the 100 games with the most recently verified runs as of 25 May 2026 — not the 100 most-popular games, not the 100 most-iconic, not the 100 with the most lifetime runs. This is a moving window. Three populations dominate the cut: (1) brand-new releases whose communities are still onboarding (Subnautica 2 hit Early Access on 14 May 2026, eleven days before the fetch, and tops the list); (2) recent blockbusters where the meta is still being figured out (Hollow Knight: Silksong, Hades 2, Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End); and (3) 'evergreen grinder' titles whose verification rate is dominated by a single dedicated community uploading hundreds of runs each (Granny: Legacy, multiple SpongeBob games, ROBLOX-engine titles, Geometry Dash). The 'casual canon' games — Super Mario 64, Hollow Knight, BotW, Undertale — appear too, but as second-rank presences rather than the top of the list.

raw_evidence.label: Origin of speedrun.com
raw_evidence.content: Speedrun.com was founded in March 2014 by Irish programmer Peter Chase, who goes by the username 'Pac'. It was designed with deliberately looser submission rules than the older Speed Demos Archive (SDA, 1998) and gave each game its own community-elected moderators rather than a single editorial board. The first migration was a wave of Grand Theft Auto runners; from there it grew into the de-facto central hub for speedrun leaderboards. In October 2020 Chase sold the site to Elo Entertainment, citing growth ambitions. By July 2021, Wikipedia reports the site hosted 'leaderboards for over 20,000 video games' — a five-year ramp from a single game's leaderboard to a multi-thousand-game commons.

raw_evidence.label: Verification: how a run becomes 'verified'
raw_evidence.content: Every run on a speedrun.com leaderboard exists in one of three states: pending, verified, or rejected. A submission must include video proof and is reviewed by the community-elected moderators of that specific game, who check splits, audio sync, glitch boundaries, and (for high-end runs) sometimes a handcam showing the player's hands on the controller. The site does not run a single global verification policy; each game's moderator team writes its own ruleset, defines its own categories, and decides what counts as proof. This is why the same dataset can contain a 4-minute Subnautica 2 glitched run and a 3-hour Silksong True Ending run, both stamped 'verified' — they are verified by completely different small teams of volunteers. The technical scaffolding that made this workable was YouTube (2005, video hosting) and Twitch (2011, livestream replays); together they let any moderator anywhere watch any submitted run frame by frame.

raw_evidence.label: What 'top-100 most active' actually selects
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is the 100 games with the most recently verified runs as of 25 May 2026 — not the 100 most-popular games, not the 100 most-iconic, not the 100 with the most lifetime runs. This is a moving window. Three populations dominate the cut: (1) brand-new releases whose communities are still onboarding (Subnautica 2 hit Early Access on 14 May 2026, eleven days before the fetch, and tops the list); (2) recent blockbusters where the meta is still being figured out (Hollow Knight: Silksong, Hades 2, Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End); and (3) 'evergreen grinder' titles whose verification rate is dominated by a single dedicated community uploading hundreds of runs each (Granny: Legacy, multiple SpongeBob games, ROBLOX-engine titles, Geometry Dash). The 'casual canon' games — Super Mario 64, Hollow Knight, BotW, Undertale — appear too, but as second-rank presences rather than the top of the list.

raw_evidence.label: Origin of speedrun.com
raw_evidence.content: Speedrun.com was founded in March 2014 by Irish programmer Peter Chase, who goes by the username 'Pac'. It was designed with deliberately looser submission rules than the older Speed Demos Archive (SDA, 1998) and gave each game its own community-elected moderators rather than a single editorial board. The first migration was a wave of Grand Theft Auto runners; from there it grew into the de-facto central hub for speedrun leaderboards. In October 2020 Chase sold the site to Elo Entertainment, citing growth ambitions. By July 2021, Wikipedia reports the site hosted 'leaderboards for over 20,000 video games' — a five-year ramp from a single game's leaderboard to a multi-thousand-game commons.

raw_evidence.label: Verification: how a run becomes 'verified'
raw_evidence.content: Every run on a speedrun.com leaderboard exists in one of three states: pending, verified, or rejected. A submission must include video proof and is reviewed by the community-elected moderators of that specific game, who check splits, audio sync, glitch boundaries, and (for high-end runs) sometimes a handcam showing the player's hands on the controller. The site does not run a single global verification policy; each game's moderator team writes its own ruleset, defines its own categories, and decides what counts as proof. This is why the same dataset can contain a 4-minute Subnautica 2 glitched run and a 3-hour Silksong True Ending run, both stamped 'verified' — they are verified by completely different small teams of volunteers. The technical scaffolding that made this workable was YouTube (2005, video hosting) and Twitch (2011, livestream replays); together they let any moderator anywhere watch any submitted run frame by frame.

raw_evidence.label: What 'top-100 most active' actually selects
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is the 100 games with the most recently verified runs as of 25 May 2026 — not the 100 most-popular games, not the 100 most-iconic, not the 100 with the most lifetime runs. This is a moving window. Three populations dominate the cut: (1) brand-new releases whose communities are still onboarding (Subnautica 2 hit Early Access on 14 May 2026, eleven days before the fetch, and tops the list); (2) recent blockbusters where the meta is still being figured out (Hollow Knight: Silksong, Hades 2, Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End); and (3) 'evergreen grinder' titles whose verification rate is dominated by a single dedicated community uploading hundreds of runs each (Granny: Legacy, multiple SpongeBob games, ROBLOX-engine titles, Geometry Dash). The 'casual canon' games — Super Mario 64, Hollow Knight, BotW, Undertale — appear too, but as second-rank presences rather than the top of the list.

raw_evidence.label: Silksong: six years of waiting, one month of records
raw_evidence.content: Hollow Knight: Silksong was announced on 14 February 2019 and released on 4 September 2025 — a wait of roughly six and a half years, during which Team Cherry's near-silence became its own running joke. The release was vertical: over 500,000 concurrent Steam players on launch day, more than 5 million distinct players in the first three days, and over 7 million copies sold by mid-December 2025. The speedrun community detonated to match. Per PC Gamer reporting on the Silksong speedrun.com leaderboards, in just one month after launch Silksong had 'more active runners than every other game on Speedrun.com, including Celeste and ULTRAKILL'. The Any% world record was driven from no-record to 1:08:15 to 1:03:41 (both by runner Blue / BlueSR) within weeks. This single release explains a meaningful chunk of the top-100 verification activity in our dataset.

The release was vertical: over 500,000 concurrent Steam players on launch day, more than 5 million distinct players in the first three days, and over 7 million copies sold by mid-December 2025. The speedrun community detonated to match. Per PC Gamer reporting on the Silksong speedrun.com leaderboards, in just one month after launch Silksong had 'more active runners than every other game on Speedrun.com, including Celeste and ULTRAKILL'. The Any% world record was driven from no-record to 1:08:15 to 1:03:41 (both by runner Blue / BlueSR) within weeks. This single release explains a meaningful chunk of the top-100 verification activity in our dataset.

raw_evidence.label: Silksong median Any% time: 83 minutes at launch, ~65 minutes by spring 2026
raw_evidence.content: Track the median Any% submission time week-by-week and the community's collective speedup is visible. In the launch week (29 September 2025) the median Any% Silksong submission was 4,975 seconds — 82.9 minutes. By 10 November 2025 it had dropped to 68.4 minutes, by 2 February 2026 to 61.4 minutes, and by 2 March 2026 to 60.5 minutes. The curve roughly plateaued from there: the last several weeks in our cut sit in a 58-72 minute median band. Across eight months, the typical Any% submission shrank by about 22 minutes (a 27% reduction) — the route is now well-understood, and the gains are getting marginal.

# --- ana_24: median run time per week — does the community as a whole get faster? ---

    print(f"  {w.date()}: median {t:.0f}s ({t/60:.1f}m)  (n={int(weekly.get(w, 0))})")

The other names at the top of Silksong's prolific list — meemeee (USA), CYV_ (Spain), IDAX1224 (China), 8Biggy (Quebec) — have submitted 5-9 runs each, several with sub-9-minute bests, which strongly suggests glitched or out-of-bounds sub-routes are mixed into the Any% category.

raw_evidence.label: Silksong: six years of waiting, one month of records
raw_evidence.content: Hollow Knight: Silksong was announced on 14 February 2019 and released on 4 September 2025 — a wait of roughly six and a half years, during which Team Cherry's near-silence became its own running joke. The release was vertical: over 500,000 concurrent Steam players on launch day, more than 5 million distinct players in the first three days, and over 7 million copies sold by mid-December 2025. The speedrun community detonated to match. Per PC Gamer reporting on the Silksong speedrun.com leaderboards, in just one month after launch Silksong had 'more active runners than every other game on Speedrun.com, including Celeste and ULTRAKILL'. The Any% world record was driven from no-record to 1:08:15 to 1:03:41 (both by runner Blue / BlueSR) within weeks. This single release explains a meaningful chunk of the top-100 verification activity in our dataset.

raw_evidence.label: SpongeBob: an unlikely speedrun dynasty
raw_evidence.content: Eight separate SpongeBob entries appear in our top-100 ('Battle for Bikini Bottom' original and Rehydrated, plus Category Extensions for both, 'Cosmic Shake', 'Titans of the Tide', 'Big Guy Challenge', 'Basics! - Remastered', 'Destroy SpongeBob'). The series became a speedrun anchor after 'Battle for Bikini Bottom' was performed at AGDQ 2017 by the runner SHIFT, and PC Gamer profiled the community in 2020 as 'a surprisingly compelling bracket packed with enough nuance to seduce any aspiring speed player.' What this tells us about our top-100 cut: a single dedicated community can keep a 22-year-old kids' platformer above 'Super Mario 64' in terms of recent verification activity. The currently-most-active list rewards active grinders, not historical fame.

raw_evidence.label: The lens: a snapshot of what people are grinding right now
raw_evidence.content: Put items det_04 through det_09 together and the dataset reveals its true subject: this is not a 'best games to speedrun' census, it is a snapshot of the speedrunning labour pool's attention in May 2026. Three forces shape the picture. First, a megalaunch (Silksong; Subnautica 2 EA) pulls dozens of runners onto a single leaderboard for weeks. Second, an entrenched grind (Granny: Legacy, SpongeBob, ROBLOX Speed Run 4, Geometry Dash) keeps a small dedicated cohort uploading runs at a steady rate. Third, infrastructure events (GDQ marathons; Discord category resets; rule revisions like the Silksong DLC patch coming in 2026) periodically flood verification queues. A good blog should treat this as a labour-market document, not a hall of fame.

raw_evidence.label: Granny: Legacy growth curve: 1 run to ~900 runs/month in 15 months
raw_evidence.content: The Granny: Legacy leaderboard opened in February 2025 with a single verified run. By month, the growth has been near-exponential: 4 runs in March, 12 in April, then plateauing for several months at 26-29/month through summer 2025. The jump came in October 2025 (68 runs), then 134 in November, 292 in December. 2026 has been: January 501, February 707, March 763, April 899 (peak month so far). The first three weeks of May 2026 saw 475 — pacing to match or beat April. Almost no other speedrun community in the dataset has grown this fast from a standing start.
raw_evidence.code:
for m, n in monthly.items():
    print(f"  {m.strftime('%Y-%m')}\t{n}")

# --- ana_31: Granny: Legacy monthly profile from leaderboard birth (2025-02) ---
print("=== ana_31 ===")
granny_id = games[games["name"] == "Granny: Legacy"]["game_id"].iloc[0]
gr = runs[runs["game_id"] == granny_id].copy()
gr["month"] = gr["date_verified"].dt.to_period("M").dt.start_time
gm = gr.groupby("month").size()
for m, n in gm.items():
    print(f"  {m.strftime('%Y-%m')}\t{n}")

raw_evidence.label: Last 30 days: Granny: Legacy alone is 25%
raw_evidence.content: Of the 2,230 runs verified in the last 30 days before the fetch (26 April → 25 May 2026), Granny: Legacy is single-handedly responsible for 561 — over 25% of the entire top-100 verification activity. Hollow Knight: Silksong is next at 125 (5.6%), then Super Mario 64 (113), Hades 2 (90), Poppy Playtime: Chapter 1 (87), Block Tales (79). A single Slavic-dominated mobile horror leaderboard is contributing more verifications than the next four games combined.

No other game in the top-100 has anything close to this kind of single-region capture.

raw_evidence.label: The lens: a snapshot of what people are grinding right now
raw_evidence.content: Put items det_04 through det_09 together and the dataset reveals its true subject: this is not a 'best games to speedrun' census, it is a snapshot of the speedrunning labour pool's attention in May 2026. Three forces shape the picture. First, a megalaunch (Silksong; Subnautica 2 EA) pulls dozens of runners onto a single leaderboard for weeks. Second, an entrenched grind (Granny: Legacy, SpongeBob, ROBLOX Speed Run 4, Geometry Dash) keeps a small dedicated cohort uploading runs at a steady rate. Third, infrastructure events (GDQ marathons; Discord category resets; rule revisions like the Silksong DLC patch coming in 2026) periodically flood verification queues. A good blog should treat this as a labour-market document, not a hall of fame.

raw_evidence.label: March 2026 peak month: SpongeBob BFBB + Granny
raw_evidence.content: The all-time peak month for verification activity (3,151 runs in March 2026) was dominated by two games. SpongeBob SquarePants: Battle for Bikini Bottom contributed 1,065 runs (33.8% of the entire month) — almost certainly an organized community event. Granny: Legacy contributed 763 (24.2%). Together, those two games produced 58% of March 2026's verifications. No other single game cleared 6%. This is the clearest evidence in the dataset that the 'most-active' picture is set by a handful of marathon-organizing communities, not by what most players have ever heard of.

# --- ana_28: drivers of the 2026-03 peak month ---

print(f"2026-03 total: {len(mar)}")

The currently-most-active list rewards active grinders, not historical fame.

raw_evidence.label: 92% of runners speedrun exactly one game
raw_evidence.content: Of 28,069 distinct registered runners in the dataset, 25,863 (92.1%) have submitted verified runs in only one game. 1,758 (6.3%) cover two games. 439 (1.6%) cover three to five games. Only 9 runners — barely 0.03% — cover six or more games, with Akuretaki at the extreme (11 games). The mean is 1.10 games per runner; the median is 1. The picture this paints: even though the top-100 cut spans 100 games, almost everyone in it is a specialist who lives in one game's community.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_20: how many distinct games per runner ---
print("=== ana_20 ===")
games_per_runner = reg.groupby("player_id")["game_id"].nunique()
print(f"Mean games per runner: {games_per_runner.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Median games per runner: {int(games_per_runner.median())}")
print(f"Runners with 1 game only:  {(games_per_runner == 1).sum()} ({100*(games_per_runner == 1).mean():4.1f}%)")
print(f"Runners with 2 games:      {(games_per_runner == 2).sum()} ({100*(games_per_runner == 2).mean():4.1f}%)")
print(f"Runners with 3-5 games:    {((games_per_runner >= 3) & (games_per_runner <= 5)).sum()} ({100*((games_per_runner >= 3) & (games_per_runner <= 5)).mean():4.1f}%)")
print(f"Runners with 6+ games:     {(games_per_runner >= 6).sum()} ({100*(games_per_runner >= 6).mean():4.1f}%)")
print(f"Max games one runner does: {int(games_per_runner.max())}")

raw_evidence.label: The labour distribution: top 5% of runners do a third of all runs
raw_evidence.content: The runs-per-runner distribution is extremely skewed. Among the 28,069 registered runners with at least one run, the top 1% (280 runners) contribute 16.5% of all runs. The top 5% (1,403 runners) contribute 33.7%. The top 10% contribute 44.6%. The top 50% contribute 76.8%. The median runner has just 1 verified run; the 95th-percentile runner has 6; the 99th has 17; the single maximum is 315 (Akuretaki). The Lorenz curve is sharper than most labour-market distributions in the wild and roughly matches the 'Pareto principle' for the top 20% (which contributes 57.7% of runs — closer to 60/20 than 80/20).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_19: Lorenz-style concentration — what fraction of runs do the top X% of runners contribute? ---
print("=== ana_19 ===")
sorted_counts = prolific.sort_values(ascending=False).values
cum = np.cumsum(sorted_counts)
total_runs = cum[-1]
n_runners = len(sorted_counts)
for pct in [1, 5, 10, 20, 50]:
    k = max(1, int(n_runners * pct / 100))
    share = 100 * cum[k - 1] / total_runs
    print(f"  top {pct:>2}% of runners ({k:>5}) account for {share:5.1f}% of runs")
print(f"\nMedian runs per runner: {int(np.median(sorted_counts))}")
print(f"75th percentile:         {int(np.percentile(sorted_counts, 75))}")
print(f"95th percentile:         {int(np.percentile(sorted_counts, 95))}")
print(f"99th percentile:         {int(np.percentile(sorted_counts, 99))}")
print(f"Max single runner runs:  {int(sorted_counts[0])}")

# Save Lorenz data for the chart (every 1% bucket)
print("\nLorenz curve data (rounded to 1% buckets):")
xs = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
ys = []
for x in xs:
    k = int(round(x * n_runners))
    if k == 0:
        ys.append(0.0)
    else:
        ys.append(100 * cum[k - 1] / total_runs)
print(f"  X (runner percentile, 0..100): generated 101 points")
print(f"  Y (cumulative run share %):    {ys[:5]} ... {ys[-5:]}")

raw_evidence.label: Verification: how a run becomes 'verified'
raw_evidence.content: Every run on a speedrun.com leaderboard exists in one of three states: pending, verified, or rejected. A submission must include video proof and is reviewed by the community-elected moderators of that specific game, who check splits, audio sync, glitch boundaries, and (for high-end runs) sometimes a handcam showing the player's hands on the controller. The site does not run a single global verification policy; each game's moderator team writes its own ruleset, defines its own categories, and decides what counts as proof. This is why the same dataset can contain a 4-minute Subnautica 2 glitched run and a 3-hour Silksong True Ending run, both stamped 'verified' — they are verified by completely different small teams of volunteers. The technical scaffolding that made this workable was YouTube (2005, video hosting) and Twitch (2011, livestream replays); together they let any moderator anywhere watch any submitted run frame by frame.

raw_evidence.label: Super Mario 64 is still 91% Nintendo 64 — but 40% of those are emulated
raw_evidence.content: Drilling into one canonical N64-era game: of the 4,403 verified Super Mario 64 runs in our cut, 3,997 (90.8%) are on the original Nintendo 64 platform, 341 (7.7%) on Wii Virtual Console, 45 (1.0%) on Switch, and 20 (0.5%) on Wii U Virtual Console. But within the N64 cohort, 40.4% of runs are flagged as emulated rather than performed on real cartridge hardware. So 'Super Mario 64 on N64' on the leaderboards today is roughly a 60/40 split between original-hardware and Project64/Mupen64/etc. The overall emulator share for SM64 (across all platforms, including VC which is itself emulation) is 36.7%.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_16: Super Mario 64 platform mix (the canonical N64-era classic) ---
print("=== ana_16 ===")
sm64_id = games[games["name"] == "Super Mario 64"]["game_id"].iloc[0]
sm64 = runs[runs["game_id"] == sm64_id]
sm64_plat = sm64["platform_name"].fillna("(unknown)").value_counts()
sm64_emu = sm64.groupby("platform_name")["emulated"].mean() * 100
print(f"Super Mario 64 runs: {len(sm64)}, distinct platforms: {sm64_plat.size}")
for p, n in sm64_plat.items():
    e = sm64_emu.get(p, float("nan"))
    print(f"  {n:>4} ({100*n/len(sm64):4.1f}%)  {p}  (emu {e:5.1f}%)")
overall_emu_pct = 100 * sm64["emulated"].mean()
print(f"\nOverall SM64 emulator share: {overall_emu_pct:.1f}% ({sm64['emulated'].sum()} of {len(sm64)})")

  3997 (90.8%)  Nintendo 64  (emu  40.4%)

    45 ( 1.0%)  Switch  (emu   0.0%)
    20 ( 0.5%)  Wii U Virtual Console  (emu   0.0%)

raw_evidence.content: Every run on a speedrun.com leaderboard exists in one of three states: pending, verified, or rejected. A submission must include video proof and is reviewed by the community-elected moderators of that specific game, who check splits, audio sync, glitch boundaries, and (for high-end runs) sometimes a handcam showing the player's hands on the controller. The site does not run a single global verification policy; each game's moderator team writes its own ruleset, defines its own categories, and decides what counts as proof. This is why the same dataset can contain a 4-minute Subnautica 2 glitched run and a 3-hour Silksong True Ending run, both stamped 'verified' — they are verified by completely different small teams of volunteers. The technical scaffolding that made this workable was YouTube (2005, video hosting) and Twitch (2011, livestream replays); together they let any moderator anywhere watch any submitted run frame by frame.

sources.title: Speedrunning — Wikipedia
facts: Submissions are 'reviewed by moderators of each game in the community' before a run becomes verified
Stricter competitions require 'a video of the hands on the controller or keyboard' (handcam)
YouTube (2005) and Twitch (2011) are cited as the platforms that 'enabled speedrun sharing' and 'facilitated livestream verification'
Detection methods include 'forensic audio analysis and mathematical analysis of probability'
